The Reform Party, founded by Texas billionaire Ross Perot in 1995. A centrist third party focused on federal deficit reduction, campaign finance reform, and fiscal responsibility, it ran Perot as its presidential candidate in 1996.

Perot had first run in 1992 as an independent, winning an extraordinary 18.9 percent of the popular vote by emphasizing the national debt and critiquing the two-party duopoly. His strong performance energized supporters to formally establish the Reform Party for 1996. The party's platform prioritized reducing the federal deficit, eliminating the national debt over a fixed timeline, implementing campaign finance reform, and imposing term limits for Congress.

Perot's 1996 Reform Party candidacy netted 8.4 percent of the popular vote and no electoral votes, the strongest third-party showing since Theodore Roosevelt's 1912 Bull Moose campaign. He appealed to fiscally conservative voters alienated from both major parties but could not achieve durable organizational strength. Perot was a charismatic but erratic candidate whose charts-and-graphs populism, popularized through infomercials, resonated with voters fed up with conventional politics and concerned about national fiscal health.

The party quickly declined after Perot's loss. It fractured over whether to seek a moderate Republican direction or a progressive populist one. By 2000, it was factionalized and moribund. Donald Trump's 2016 and 2020 campaigns drew some former Reform Party voters, but the party itself never revived. The Reform Party exemplifies how charisma-dependent third parties often collapse when their founder departs, despite once commanding substantial support.
